title: Unit 1: Money Basics
subtitle: Budgeting, saving, and everyday money habits

questions.prompt: What is a budget?
choices: A plan for how you'll spend and save your money
questions.explanation: A budget is simply a plan that maps out your income and expenses so you know where your money is going.

questions.prompt: A budget should include both your income and your expenses.
questions.explanation: A good budget tracks money coming in (income) and money going out (expenses).

questions.prompt: Sort each item into fixed (same every month) or variable (changes month to month).
questions.explanation: Fixed costs like rent and insurance stay the same; variable costs like groceries and dining out move around with your choices.

questions.prompt: You earn $2,000 a month and spend $2,300. How many dollars over budget are you?
questions.explanation: Spending $2,300 on $2,000 of income is a $300 deficit. You're relying on savings or debt to cover the gap.

questions.prompt: The 50/30/20 rule suggests 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
questions.explanation: It's a popular, simple guideline for splitting take-home pay across needs, wants, and savings.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in the 'needs' bucket of a budget? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Rent, groceries, and utilities are essentials. Concert tickets are a 'want': nice, but not required to live.

questions.prompt: Put these budgeting steps in the order you'd do them.
items: Adjust spending to hit your savings goal
questions.explanation: Start with what comes in, list what goes out, find the difference, then adjust. That's the budgeting loop.

questions.prompt: Drop each purchase into 'Need' or 'Want'.
questions.explanation: Needs keep you fed, housed, and able to earn. Wants add enjoyment but you could live without them.

questions.prompt: Streaming subscriptions are usually considered a 'want.'
questions.explanation: Enjoyable, but not essential to survive, so streaming is generally a want.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to separate needs from wants?
choices: It helps you cover essentials first and avoid debt
It has no real impact on your finances
questions.explanation: Knowing the difference makes sure essentials are paid for before extras. That's the core of not overspending.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a 'want'?
choices: Something that improves life but isn't essential to survive
Something you must have to survive
questions.explanation: Wants add comfort or fun; you could go without them if money got tight.

questions.prompt: Match each item to whether it's usually a need or a want.
questions.explanation: Health and staying warm are needs; extra entertainment and upgrades are wants.

questions.prompt: Housing and basic utilities are usually considered needs.
questions.explanation: Shelter, water, heat, and electricity are essentials. They're classic needs.

questions.prompt: Using the 50/30/20 rule on $2,000 take-home pay, how many dollars go to 'wants'?
questions.explanation: 30% of $2,000 is $600, the slice the rule sets aside for wants.

questions.prompt: What is an emergency fund for?
choices: Unexpected costs like medical bills or car repairs
questions.explanation: It's a cushion for life's surprises, not for planned spending.

questions.prompt: Experts often suggest saving how many months of expenses in an emergency fund? (Give the low end of the common 3–6 range.)
questions.explanation: 3–6 months of expenses is the usual target; 3 months is a solid starting goal.

questions.prompt: Where should you generally NOT keep your emergency fund?
choices: In risky stocks that can drop fast
questions.explanation: Emergency money must be safe and easy to reach, not tied up in something that could fall right when you need it.

questions.prompt: What does 'paying yourself first' mean?
choices: Setting aside savings before spending on anything else
Investing all your income in stocks
questions.explanation: Automate savings before you can spend the money. It's gone before you miss it.

questions.prompt: An emergency fund should be easy to access quickly if needed.
questions.explanation: Liquidity matters. In a real emergency you need the cash fast.

questions.prompt: Order these savings priorities from what most people should do first to last.
items: Grow the fund to 3–6 months of expenses
Start investing for the long term
questions.explanation: A starter cushion first, then pay off high-interest debt, then a full emergency fund, then invest. That's a common order.

questions.prompt: If your essential expenses are $1,500 a month, how big is a 3-month emergency fund?
questions.explanation: $1,500 × 3 months = $4,500, enough to cover three months of essentials.

questions.prompt: Match each account or term to what it's for.
pairs: Setting money aside to earn interest
Yearly interest a savings account pays
questions.explanation: Checking is for daily use, savings earns interest (measured as APY), and an overdraft is spending past your balance.

questions.prompt: A high-yield savings account usually pays more interest than a regular checking account.
questions.explanation: High-yield savings accounts exist to grow your cash; checking is built for spending and pays little or nothing.

questions.prompt: In the U.S., what does FDIC insurance protect?
choices: Your bank deposits (up to the limit) if the bank fails
Your stocks if they lose value
questions.explanation: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank. Crypto and stocks don't have that safety net.

questions.prompt: What is an overdraft fee?
choices: A charge for spending more than your account balance
A fee for checking your balance
questions.explanation: Spend past your balance and many banks charge an overdraft fee, often $30 or more each time.

questions.prompt: You keep $2,000 in a savings account earning 4% APY. Roughly how many dollars of interest is that in one year?
questions.explanation: 4% of $2,000 is about $80 a year, free money for keeping your cash in the right account.

questions.prompt: Which habits help you avoid unnecessary bank fees? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Keep enough balance to avoid overdrafts
questions.explanation: Watching your balance, using in-network ATMs, and alerts all prevent fees. Ignoring the account is how fees sneak up on you.

questions.prompt: Money in a checking account is a good long-term investment for growing wealth.
questions.explanation: Checking pays little to no interest, so inflation slowly erodes it. It's for spending; invest longer-term money elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is 'impulse spending'?
choices: Buying on a whim without planning it
questions.explanation: Impulse buys are unplanned purchases made in the moment, the enemy of a budget.

questions.prompt: The '24-hour rule' for shopping means…
choices: Waiting a day before a non-essential purchase to see if you still want it
Only shopping for 24 hours a year
questions.explanation: Sleeping on it filters out impulse buys. A lot of 'must-haves' feel optional the next day.

questions.prompt: A $6 coffee bought every weekday. Roughly how many dollars is that over a 4-week month? (5 days × 4 weeks)
questions.explanation: $6 × 5 × 4 = $120 a month. Small daily buys add up fast. That's the 'latte factor.'

questions.prompt: Sort these into smart-spending habits vs. money traps.
questions.explanation: Lists and price comparison protect your money; chasing 'sales' and minimum payments quietly drain it.

questions.prompt: A sale is only a good deal if it's something you were already going to buy.
questions.explanation: Spending $40 to 'save' $10 on something you didn't need still costs you $40. A deal only helps on real needs.

questions.prompt: Why are forgotten subscriptions a common money leak?
choices: They quietly charge you every month whether you use them or not
questions.explanation: Auto-renewing subscriptions bill you on autopilot. Reviewing them a few times a year plugs the leak.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for making a smart big purchase.
items: Decide if it's a need or a want
Wait a day, then buy if it still makes sense
questions.explanation: Need vs. want, then a budget, then comparison, then a cool-off: a simple guardrail against overspending.

questions.prompt: A budget is best described as…
choices: A plan for spending and saving your money
questions.explanation: It's your money plan: income in, expenses out.

questions.prompt: Sort each into Need or Want.
questions.explanation: Essentials to live are needs; everything that just adds enjoyment is a want.

questions.prompt: Using 50/30/20 on $3,000 take-home, how many dollars should go to savings?
questions.explanation: 20% of $3,000 is $600 for savings.

questions.prompt: An emergency fund should be kept in risky stocks for higher returns.
questions.explanation: Emergency money must be safe and liquid. Stocks can drop right when you need it.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.explanation: These are the core money-basics terms from this unit.

questions.prompt: Essentials are $1,200/month. How big is a 3-month emergency fund?
Which help you avoid debt and fees? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Saving first, lists, and tracking your balance all help. Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt longer.

questions.prompt: FDIC insurance protects bank deposits up to a limit if the bank fails.
questions.explanation: Up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank: a safety net bank accounts have.

questions.prompt: Order the budgeting steps.
items: Adjust to hit your savings goal
questions.explanation: Income, expenses, difference, adjust: the budgeting loop.

questions.prompt: 'Paying yourself first' means…
questions.explanation: Save first, automatically, then spend what's left.
